Where Does Social Reasoning Come From?
Capability Provenance in Language Models

Glenn Matlin ††thanks: Corresponding author: glenn@gatech.edu Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing Affiliation: MATS Program Affiliation: Georgia Tech AI Safety Initiative    Chandreyi Chakraborty Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing    Saehee Eom Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing    Mika Okamoto Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing    Rayan Castilla Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing    Louis Jaburi Affiliation: MATS Program Affiliation: EleutherAI    Alvin Deng Affiliation: EleutherAI    Taywon Min Affiliation: MATS Program Affiliation: KAIST AI    Lucia Quirke Affiliation: MATS Program Affiliation: EleutherAI    Stella Biderman Affiliation: EleutherAI    Mark Riedl Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing
Abstract

We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model’s predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer’s 24-format ×\times 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2×22{\times}2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

1 Introduction

Training-data attribution (TDA) methods estimate how much each training example influences a model’s predictions—quantifying which documents in the pretraining corpus matter most for a given behavior. Recent work using influence estimates has shown that knowledge-oriented tasks tend to rely on fewer documents, while reasoning tasks draw support from broader regions of the training corpus (Ruis et al., 2025). However, these analyses operate at the document level—showing how influence is distributed across training documents rather than identifying where in the corpus distinct capabilities, such as social versus STEM reasoning, are supported by different regions of pretraining data.

Understanding this mapping is critical for auditing and controlling model behavior: identifiable corpus regions enable inspection, modification, or reweighting to shape performance. We treat aggregate gradient-based attribution as a coarse mechanistic decomposition—a window onto the structures the model’s internal computations rely on—complementing internal-state methods (probes, circuits, dictionary learning) by analyzing inputs rather than activations. Realizing this requires moving beyond document-level estimates (Basu et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024) and coarse corpus documentation (Bender & Friedman, 2018; Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019) toward structured taxonomy-based aggregation.

Contributions.

We study capability provenance with gradient-based corpus-scale training-data attribution, structured taxonomic aggregation, and a fully-open data ecosystem. The paper makes four independent contributions:

  • •

    Bin-level aggregation as a discovery method. We aggregate document-level gradient attribution over a structured WebOrganizer taxonomy (Wettig et al., 2025) (24 formats ×\times 24 topics; 576 bins), turning corpus-scale attribution into a principled, interpretable instrument for capability provenance. This contrasts with prior approaches that take top-kk influential documents and characterize them post-hoc via language models, human annotation, or other ad-hoc summarization (Ruis et al., 2025; Razeghi et al., 2024); we apply taxonomic decomposition before inspection.

  • •

    2×22{\times}2 contrastive factorial design. We decouple capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge) from domain (social vs. STEM) within a single open ecosystem (OLMo3-7B/Dolma3 (Ettinger et al., 2025; Soldaini et al., 2024)), using SocialIQA (Sap et al., 2019), MMLU Social Sciences (Hendrycks et al., 2021), ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), and MMLU STEM (Hendrycks et al., 2021) as the four cells. The factorial structure lets us measure whether capability type or domain better explains corpus-level differentiation.

  • •

    Lexical profiling of high-influence bins. We connect bin-level provenance to surface text features, using transparent counters and Empath enrichment (Fast et al., 2016) for pronoun density, mental-state-verb density, and dialogue indicators, revealing a bimodal lexical signature for social-reasoning influence: short interpersonal text and long-form documentation both contribute.

  • •

    Targeted unlearning validation. Influence-targeted unlearning (Zhao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025) of high-attribution bins degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and across benchmarks produces a controllable selective damage profile rather than generic degradation.

All code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints are openly released, in keeping with the paper’s open-data-and-open-source methodological commitment.

We study capability provenance in the open OLMo ecosystem (Soldaini et al., 2024; Groeneveld et al., 2024) using Bergson (Quirke et al., 2026) gradient-based attribution over a stratified working set of 5,678,6215,678,621 documents (10.5B tokens; 10,00010,000/bin) from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix of 1,263,587,1681,263,587,168 (∼{\sim}1.26B) unique documents. WebOrganizer (Wettig et al., 2025) assigns each document a topic (e.g., Social Life, Literature, Software Development) and a format (e.g., Q&A Forum, Customer Support, Documentation). Our attribution unit is the resulting topic–format bin (24 ×\times 24 = 576 bins), such as Social Life ×\times Q&A Forum or Literature ×\times Customer Support; the full taxonomy appears in Appendix A. We choose the four primary benchmarks as a controlled OLMES-compatible 2×22{\times}2, not a loose task suite: domain (social vs. STEM) crossed with capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge) (Gu et al., 2025). The reasoning cells are SocialIQA (Sap et al., 2019) and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), which ask likelihood-scored multiple-choice questions over social commonsense narratives and multi-step scientific problems; the knowledge cells are MMLU Social Sciences and MMLU STEM (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Because all four targets are fixed-choice, above-chance OLMo3 evaluations under the same protocol, this pairing lets us ask whether corpus regions separate by domain, by capability type, or by their interaction (Figure 1).

The resulting distributions show that social and non-social benchmarks draw support from markedly different corpus regions, in patterns that are consistent across benchmarks and interpretable. We validate these associations via targeted unlearning.

We frame the study around three research questions, progressing from description to comparison to unlearning validation:

  • •

    Where does each benchmark’s attribution concentrate in the topic×\timesformat taxonomy, and do social and STEM benchmarks show distinct profiles?

  • •

    Do social- and STEM-reasoning benchmarks draw attribution from different corpus regions, and does the same hold for the knowledge pair?

  • •

    Are high-attribution bins validated by targeted unlearning? Does unlearning these bins degrade the aligned benchmark more than contrastive controls?

Our findings show that social reasoning and STEM reasoning in OLMo3-7B draw on qualitatively different regions of the Dolma3 training corpus, and that social reasoning and social-domain knowledge, while both in the social domain, exhibit distinguishable attribution profiles—extending evidence that different capabilities can depend on different pretraining evidence (Ruis et al., 2025; Antoniades et al., 2024; Razeghi et al., 2024), with targeted machine unlearning providing partial validation (Zhao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025).

2 Related Work

Training-data attribution and aggregation in language models. Training-data attribution identifies which corpus parts shape model behavior. Classical influence functions estimate up-weighting effects without retraining (Koh & Liang, 2017); later work introduced scalable gradient-based approximations such as TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020) and TRAK (Park et al., 2023), with improved inverse-Hessian methods for large models (Schioppa et al., 2022; Grosse et al., 2023). Subsequent research traces model outputs or factual knowledge back to training data (Akyurek et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2025) and builds retrieval or indexing systems for corpus-scale attribution (Lin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Concurrently, prior work identifies limitations of example-level estimates: brittleness to approximation choices (Basu et al., 2021; Grosse et al., 2023), failure to capture interactions between training examples (Guu et al., 2023), and inconsistent cross-task behavior (Jiao et al., 2025).

Faced with these limitations, recent corpus-attribution work for capability provenance has converged on two limited paths. The first takes the top-kk influential documents for a behavior of interest and characterizes them post-hoc—via language models, human annotation, or other ad-hoc summarization (Ruis et al., 2025; Razeghi et al., 2024)—which recovers which documents matter but is descriptive rather than principled, with the characterization step itself a source of noise. The second performs machine unlearning on putative dataset components (Zhao et al., 2024), but on closed-data models this requires proxy datasets that may diverge from the actual pretraining distribution. We instead apply structured taxonomic decomposition (WebOrganizer (Wettig et al., 2025)) before inspection, on the released pretraining corpus—to our knowledge the first application of gradient-based corpus-scale TDA to capability provenance with taxonomic aggregation on a fully-open data ecosystem.

Open corpora, model transparency, and data documentation. Our approach relies on an open-model ecosystem in which the pretraining corpus, training pipeline, and model checkpoints are all accessible at the document level. Resources such as Dolma (Soldaini et al., 2024) and OLMo3 (Ettinger et al., 2025) enable direct study of how pretraining data shapes model behavior, which is infeasible for closed-data models. We emphasize that open-weight and open-data are distinct: models that publish weights without their pretraining corpora (Longpre et al., 2024) are unsuitable targets for document-level gradient-based attribution regardless of weight openness. Among models meeting the joint open-data, open-checkpoint, and open-tokenizer requirements (OLMo, Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), the Common Pile-trained models (Kandpal et al., 2025)), OLMo3 currently has the most comprehensive evaluation methodology (OLMES; Gu et al., 2025). Our work builds on this transparency agenda by connecting benchmark behavior to attributable regions of the training corpus.

Machine unlearning as validation. Attribution scores are associational: a high influence score suggests that a training region matters, but does not prove it. Machine unlearning offers a complementary, interventionist test—if a corpus region genuinely supports a capability, then forgetting that region should degrade the capability while leaving unrelated benchmarks intact. Recent work explores unlearning for analyzing training data effects. NGDiff (Jin et al., 2025) uses gradient-normalized objectives with LoRA to forget targeted data without catastrophic loss of general ability, and Zhao et al. (2024) show that unlearning specific pretraining slices can reveal which data components drive downstream task performance. We adopt this approach to validate our strongest attribution findings, treating bin-level unlearning as a counterpart to the influence analysis.

How capabilities depend on training data. We ask whether different capability families—such as social reasoning, social-domain knowledge, and quantitative reasoning—draw support from systematically different regions of pretraining data. Recent tracing work shows that capabilities depend on distinct types of pretraining evidence (Ruis et al., 2025), that memorization and generalization can be analyzed via attribution (Antoniades et al., 2024), and that mathematical reasoning can be traced to specific data sources (Razeghi et al., 2024). We extend this line of work by examining whether such distinctions emerge at aggregate corpus level, revealing how capabilities are supported.

3 Method

We study capability provenance through data attribution, using targeted benchmarks as queries against an open-data model, complemented by validation via machine unlearning.

3.1 Corpus Construction

Training data attribution requires a model family whose pretraining corpus and checkpoints are both released. We therefore use the OLMo3-7B open-data ecosystem (Ettinger et al., 2025): OLMo3-7B Base is the object of pretraining-data attribution over Dolma3, while OLMo3-7B Instruct supplies the benchmark completions and query gradients used for scoring. This split follows the base-document/instruct-query design of Ruis et al. (2025): document gradients and corpus-side curvature are computed on Base so the index remains tied to pretraining data, whereas query gradients are computed on Instruct because it follows the OLMES multiple-choice and chat-style prompts more reliably.

Data De-duplication & Taxonomy Enrichment

The 6T token mix was generated with quality-aware up-sampling, in which higher-quality data is replicated more frequently in the training mixture to increase its effective weight (Soldaini et al., 2024). We de-duplicated the dataset to avoid duplicate attributions from up-sampled documents. We then classify the Common Crawl and olmOCR portions of the de-duplicated corpus (1,098,646,1621,098,646,162 documents, ∼87%{\sim}87\% of the population) with topic and format classifiers from WebOrganizer (Wettig et al., 2025), yielding taxonomies of 2424 topics ×\times 2424 formats, resulting in 576 bins. The remaining code, mathematics, and reference families (Stack-Edu, FineMath, arXiv, Wikipedia) are retained in the population count but not taxonomized, since the web-oriented WebOrganizer taxonomy does not apply to them. These bins provide a structured view of the corpus, enabling comparison across diverse semantic bins.

Stratified Sampling

We estimate influence on a stratified sample of the de-duplicated dataset, ensuring equal representation across taxonomy bins. The Dolma3 corpus (Soldaini et al., 2024) exhibits substantial skew, so naive sampling would under-sample low-volume bins and yield unstable gradient estimates (see Appendices B.2 and B.3). To address this, we construct a balanced working set by uniformly sampling from each bin, enabling cross-bin comparisons.

3.2 Training Data Attribution

With the stratified corpus established, we define the attribution queries. Each benchmark sample serves as a query to the attribution pipeline.

Evaluation Design

We adopt a 2×22\times 2 contrastive design crossing domain (social vs. STEM) with capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge), shown in Table 1. The four cells use established OLMES-compatible benchmarks (Gu et al., 2025): SocialIQA for social commonsense reasoning (Sap et al., 2019), ARC-Challenge for science reasoning (Clark et al., 2018), and MMLU subdomains for social-science and STEM knowledge (Hendrycks et al., 2021). The reasoning/knowledge contrast is motivated by recent evidence that different capability families can draw on different kinds of pretraining evidence (Ruis et al., 2025; Antoniades et al., 2024; Razeghi et al., 2024).

This design distinguishes domain-specific effects (social vs. STEM), capability-specific effects (reasoning vs. knowledge), and domain-general patterns shared across all benchmarks. All four benchmarks are part of the OLMo 3 base evaluation suite, evaluated with OLMES (Gu et al., 2025) following the exact protocol used during model development (details in Appendix C).

Attribution Approach

With the benchmarks established, we compute document-level attribution scores using TrackStar (Chang et al., 2025) as implemented in Bergson (Quirke et al., 2026). Gradient-based training-data attribution estimates how strongly each training document affects a model’s behavior on a downstream query by comparing the gradient that document would induce during training with the gradient the model produces on the query: a document whose gradients consistently align with a benchmark’s query gradients is judged to have positive influence on that benchmark, and one whose gradients consistently oppose them is judged to have negative influence. TrackStar is a scalable variant that projects these gradients into a low-rank subspace so the comparison runs at corpus scale; we use the Bergson library (v0.9.0).

Operationally, the document and query sides use different checkpoints from the same OLMo3 family. We build the corpus gradient index from OLMo3-7B Base and reduce benchmark query gradients from OLMo3-7B Instruct. The influence score therefore compares pretraining-document gradients against the instruction-tuned model’s task gradients, under the approximation used by Ruis et al. (2025) that the supervised-instruction-tuning second-order term is the identity. This keeps the scientific target on pretraining data while using the checkpoint that follows the benchmark query format most reliably. Base-query scoring was computed as a calibration variant, but all reported attribution results use this Base-document/Instruct-query setup.

Concretely, for each benchmark we estimate how strongly each training document influences model behavior with respect to that benchmark by comparing projected gradients of training documents with those of benchmark samples as queries, producing a signed influence score per document-benchmark pair. Implementation details are in Appendix C.

3.3 Influence Aggregation

Rather than interpreting individual document scores, which can be brittle under influence-function approximations and sensitive to example interactions, we aggregate attribution over taxonomy bins (Basu et al., 2021; Grosse et al., 2023; Guu et al., 2023; Jiao et al., 2025). The WebOrganizer bins provide fixed, semantically named aggregation units (Wettig et al., 2025), yielding patterns that are stable enough to interpret at corpus-region level.

Formally, for each benchmark β\beta and bin kk, we compute the mean influence s¯\bar{s}:

s¯β,k=1|Dk|​∑j∈Dk1|Qβ|​∑q∈Qβs⁡(j,q),\bar{s}_{\beta,k}=\frac{1}{|D_{k}|}\sum_{j\in D_{k}}\frac{1}{|Q_{\beta}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{\beta}}s(j,q),

where s⁡(j,q)s(j,q) is the attribution score between training document jj and benchmark query qq, QβQ_{\beta} is the set of queries for benchmark β\beta, and DkD_{k} is the set of documents in bin kk.

This produces a 576×4576\times 4 matrix of bin-level influence values, used in all subsequent analyses.

We then analyze signed and absolute influence mass to characterize how attribution concentrates across the corpus. We also assess robustness by examining rank consistency across benchmarks and by comparing signed and absolute influence distributions.

Contrastive Analysis

For each pair of benchmarks (β,β′)(\beta,\beta^{\prime}), we compute the per-bin difference Δ​zk=zβ​(k)−zβ′​(k)\Delta z_{k}=z_{\beta}(k)-z_{\beta^{\prime}}(k), where zβ​(k)z_{\beta}(k) is the standardized bin-level influence for benchmark β\beta at bin kk (computed via the aggregation rule in Section 3.3). The resulting per-bin contrastive distribution identifies domain-specific bins (large |Δ​z||\Delta z|, signaling strong influence for one benchmark only), shared bins (small |Δ​z||\Delta z| but large |z||z| for both benchmarks, signaling general capability support), and the geometric structure of how attribution mass shifts between tasks. We report bins where |Δ​z||\Delta z| exceeds the bootstrap-derived noise floor as discriminative; confidence intervals are derived from 1,000-iteration resampling over documents within bin and shown in the corresponding figures.

Correctness Stratification

For each benchmark β\beta, we partition the eval queries QβQ_{\beta} into a correct cohort Qβ+Q_{\beta}^{+} (queries the model answers correctly under standard OLMES scoring) and an incorrect cohort Qβ−Q_{\beta}^{-}. We then compute per-bin influence aggregates separately for each cohort using the same bin-level aggregation rule, yielding zβ+​(k)z_{\beta}^{+}(k) and zβ−​(k)z_{\beta}^{-}(k). The correctness differential Δ​zβc​(k)=zβ+​(k)−zβ−​(k)\Delta z^{\mathrm{c}}_{\beta}(k)=z_{\beta}^{+}(k)-z_{\beta}^{-}(k) identifies bins whose content disproportionately drives the model’s correct predictions on β\beta, separating provenance-of-capability (positive Δ​zc\Delta z^{\mathrm{c}}) from provenance-of-error (negative Δ​zc\Delta z^{\mathrm{c}}). Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals follow the same 1,000-iteration document-resampling procedure used for the contrastive analysis.

Lexical profiling.

To characterize the text in high-influence bins, we compute an open, LIWC-adjacent profile over the working set: in-repo pronoun, mental-state, function-word, and cognition counters, social/affective/topical categories from the open-source Empath analyzer (Fast et al., 2016), and direction-preserving proxies for the four LIWC summary variables (Analytic, Clout, Authentic, Tone). These are not LIWC.app outputs; the crosswalk, lexicons, and zz-scoring baselines, with the expanded characterization, are detailed in Appendix H.

3.4 Validation via Targeted Machine Unlearning

While attribution identifies associational patterns, it does not inherently show that the identified data is necessary for a given capability. We complement our influence analysis with targeted machine unlearning, treating topic-level forgetting as a diagnostic intervention, following prior uses of unlearning to analyze pretraining-data effects (Zhao et al., 2024). Our goal is to test whether corpus regions with higher attribution mass are necessary for specific capabilities. Because the causal claim concerns pretraining data, unlearning is applied to OLMo3-7B Base rather than the instruction-tuned checkpoint; this avoids treating post-training behavior as a direct forget-set target. Thus, the capability profiles reported for attribution use the deployment-realistic Instruct checkpoint, whereas the unlearning degradation γ\gamma is a base-model measurement. Following the NGDiff framework (Jin et al., 2025), we extend unlearning to the granular WebOrganizer taxonomy.

We structure these interventions around two axes: selection strategy (random vs. influence-guided) and data scope (single-topic vs. global). All unlearning runs train a rank-8 LoRA adapter on OLMo3-7B Base with the NGDiff gradient-normalized objective (Jin et al., 2025), then merge the adapter back into the base checkpoint for evaluation. We report raw accuracy damage, where positive values mean the unlearned checkpoint is less accurate than the Base checkpoint:

γ=Abaseline−Aunlearned\gamma=A_{\mathrm{baseline}}-A_{\mathrm{unlearned}}

Detailed optimization parameters, resampling strategies, and the randomized-text stopping criterion are provided in Appendix I.

3.4.1 Experimental Conditions

We compare two selection strategies against a global control. For each of the 24 topic bins, we run two paired unlearning conditions: (1) random baseline with k=2,000k{=}2{,}000 documents sampled uniformly from that bin; (2) influence-guided with the top-kk documents by Bergson influence scores for the target benchmark. These each yield a 24×424\times 4 matrix γb,j\gamma_{b,j}. A global random control samples k=2,000k{=}2{,}000 documents from the entire corpus with no topic alignment, yielding the net effect γnet=γtopic−γglobal\gamma_{\mathrm{net}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{topic}}-\gamma_{\mathrm{global}}.

4 Results

Unless otherwise noted, all influence scores reported in this section are zz-score standardized within each benchmark over WebOrganizer bins. For each benchmark, we standardize the per-bin signed mean influence scores to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 across bins; “absolute influence” refers to the absolute value of these standardized scores.

The working set contains 5,678,6215,678,621 documents (∼{\sim}10.5B tokens) stratified across 576 WebOrganizer (Wettig et al., 2025) bins (10,00010,000 per bin; see Appendix B.4 for bin fill rates).

4.1 Bin-Level Attribution Profiles

Figure 2 summarizes the qualitative pattern that distinguishes social-reasoning attribution from the other three benchmarks. In our OLMo3/Dolma3 measurements, the social-knowledge and STEM benchmarks concentrate their strongest positive influence in documentation-like formats, while SocialIQA’s strongest format marginal is Customer Support. At the topic level, Literature and Social Life are positive for SocialIQA but negative for the three comparison benchmarks. The selected cells in Panel C show that this is not only a marginal artifact: Literature ×\times Customer Support is the extreme SocialIQA-positive bin and flips negative for MMLU Social Sciences and MMLU STEM, while Social Life ×\times Q&A and Home ×\times Creative give smaller but interpretable SocialIQA-specific cells. The added near-neutral rows show that this is not a generic effect of every narrative-looking format or every human-centered topic. The full signed bin-level influence heatmaps appear in Figure 12 (Appendix D).

SocialIQA’s positive influence is distributed far more evenly across topics and formats than the other three benchmarks, whose strong positive mass concentrates in the Documentation column while News Article registers as a consistent negative (Appendix D). The single bin with the highest influence on SocialIQA is Literature ×\times Customer Support.

We also marginalize the heatmaps along each axis by averaging across formats to obtain per-topic influence, and across topics to obtain per-format influence for all benchmarks. These marginals, reported in Appendix D, show that the observed patterns are not isolated to a single extreme bin. The near-neutral Creative Writing and Transportation rows are useful negative checks: the social-reasoning signal is not simply any narrative-looking format or broad human-centered topic. A whole-profile comparison confirms the effect is not driven by one bin, with SocialIQA’s 576-bin influence profile correlating with the three comparison benchmarks at r≤0.22r\!\leq\!0.22 versus r=0.76r=0.76–0.860.86 among them, making it the only benchmark with a significant profile-divergence statistic (Appendix D.1).

At the topic level, the clearest social-reasoning divergence is the Literature sign flip: it has positive mean influence for SocialIQA while remaining among the most negatively influential topics for the other three benchmarks, and it is the strongest SocialIQA–ARC-Challenge topic contrast in Appendix E. This suggests that social reasoning performance aligns more strongly with complex literary and narrative content. In contrast, ARC-Challenge, MMLU Social Sciences, and MMLU STEM display more similar topic profiles, with Industrial and Science Math and Technology topics contributing strongly positive influence across those benchmarks but substantially less for SocialIQA.

At the format level, the distributions contain fewer but more extreme positive and negative influence values, while preserving a similar contrast between SocialIQA and the other benchmarks. Documentation is the highest-influence format for ARC-Challenge, MMLU Social Sciences, and MMLU STEM along with high-influence in Academic Writing. SocialIQA also exhibits the most distinct format profile overall, with Customer Support, FAQ, and Q&A Forum emerging as its highest-influence formats (Appendix D).

4.2 Cross-Domain Contrastive Analysis

The paired-topic heatmaps in Appendix E show a sharper social–STEM separation for reasoning (SocialIQA–ARC-Challenge) than for knowledge (MMLU Social Sciences–MMLU STEM), while preserving the same direction: Software Development tilts STEM and Education & Jobs tilts social. This suggests that, in this corpus and model, reasoning support is more domain-specific than knowledge support.

Further analyses.

Three additional analyses, detailed in the appendix, refine this picture. A correctness partition reveals a reasoning-vs-knowledge sign flip: Literature ×\times Customer Support is the top correctness-differential bin for both reasoning benchmarks (SocialIQA, ARC-Challenge) yet the strongest error-associated bin for both knowledge benchmarks (MMLU Social Sciences, MMLU STEM) (Appendix F). A wider held-out suite of social, Theory-of-Mind, moral, and pragmatic probes runs through the same pipeline as a breadth check (Appendix G). And lexical profiling shows SocialIQA’s high-influence bins are bimodal—dialogue-rich interpersonal text alongside long-form documentation (Appendix H).

4.3 Empirical Validation via Machine Unlearning

We validate the attribution results with machine unlearning, comparing influence-targeted document removal against in-topic random removal across the four benchmarks.

Across topic bins in the faithful top-200 per-document replication, influence-targeted unlearning produces larger accuracy drops than random in-topic unlearning most clearly for SocialIQA: across the available matched topic–seed cells, the paired difference γinfluence−γrandom\gamma_{\mathrm{influence}}-\gamma_{\mathrm{random}} is significantly positive (Wilcoxon BH-adjusted p≈10−5p\approx 10^{-5}; full per-benchmark statistics in Table 49 and Figure 42). MMLU-STEM is weaker: it reaches significance on the pooled Wilcoxon test, but not on the paired tt-test over topic means, and its bootstrap median interval crosses zero. MMLU-Social-Sciences does not reach significance, while ARC-Challenge has a negative median paired difference, meaning influence-targeted forgetting is slightly less damaging than random in-topic forgetting under this construction. This supports the claim that high-attribution documents identify capability-relevant corpus regions rather than only broad topic membership for SocialIQA, while the other benchmarks mark where topic-level influence does not fully isolate the relevant documents.

Appendix J reports the full unlearning suite, including convergence-speed and influence–drop diagnostics, which we treat as supporting evidence rather than separate main claims.

5 Conclusions and Future Work

Within our OLMo3-7B/Dolma3 setting, social reasoning is supported by a broader, more evenly distributed set of topic×\timesformat regions than social knowledge and STEM tasks, with targeted unlearning validating these patterns (Zhao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025).

Beyond the per-RQ takeaways above, the methodological point is that bin-level aggregation over a structured taxonomy yields stable, interpretable patterns where document-level influence scores are too brittle for reliable standalone claims (Basu et al., 2021; Grosse et al., 2023), providing actionable targets for data curation and safety-oriented auditing.

Reproducibility and Resources

All experiments use the OLMo3-7B/Dolma3 open-data ecosystem (Ettinger et al., 2025): OLMo3-7B Base anchors corpus indexing and unlearning against the deduplicated 6T Dolma3 training mix (Soldaini et al., 2024) (∼{\sim}1.26B unique documents), while OLMo3-7B Instruct supplies the benchmark completions and query gradients for attribution scoring. The reproducibility target is the full analysis workflow over the sampled working set (5,678,6215,678,621 documents, 10.5B tokens across 576 bins), not attribution over the entire upstream population. Attribution uses TrackStar (Chang et al., 2025) via Bergson v0.9.0; unlearning uses NGDiff (Jin et al., 2025) with LoRA (rank 8). The end-to-end pipeline—taxonomy enrichment of ∼{\sim}1.26B documents, gradient index construction, attribution scoring across six benchmarks, and 24-bin unlearning—consumed approximately 37,00037,000 H200 144 GB-equivalent GPU-hours (Appendix L). All pipeline parameters, compute accounting, and storage requirements are fully specified in Appendix C and I.

Following dataset and model documentation norms (Bender & Friedman, 2018; Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019), we openly release all artifacts: attribution and aggregation code, sampling scripts, bin-level manifests, the aggregate 576×4576{}\times 4 influence matrix, unlearning checkpoints, and analysis notebooks. Because the upstream Dolma3 corpus and OLMo3 weights are publicly available, the full pipeline is reproducible end-to-end. Detailed resource accounting is in Appendix C and I.

Ethics Statement

This study analyzes the relationship between pretraining data and model capabilities using publicly available resources: the open-weight OLMo3 model (Ettinger et al., 2025) and the openly released Dolma3 corpus (Soldaini et al., 2024). No new data was collected, and no human subjects were involved.

Our methodology operates at the level of aggregate corpus regions (WebOrganizer taxonomy bins) rather than individual documents, aligning the release with dataset and model documentation practices that emphasize structured disclosure over raw-example exposure (Bender & Friedman, 2018; Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019). This reduces the risk of surfacing or amplifying specific training examples. The unlearning experiments modify model behavior through parameter updates and do not alter the underlying training data.

We acknowledge that training-data attribution tools could in principle be used to identify memorized or sensitive content in pretraining corpora (Carlini et al., 2021). We mitigate this by releasing only aggregate bin-level statistics and influence matrices rather than document-level scores, and by paraphrasing any qualitative examples drawn from high-influence bins. All released artifacts are designed to support corpus-level analysis rather than individual document retrieval.

The benchmarks used in this study (SocialIQA, MMLU Social Sciences, MMLU STEM, ARC-Challenge) are established public evaluation resources (Sap et al., 2019; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2018). Our contrastive design probes the structure of capability provenance; it does not evaluate or make claims about the social reasoning abilities of any population or demographic group.
